hook.text: In German, a bridge is feminine. In Spanish it's masculine. Germans call bridges elegant; Spaniards call them strong.

buildup.text: About one-third of the world's languages assign gender to nouns. Some have two genders, others have twenty.

discovery.text: Lera Boroditsky showed speakers project human traits onto objects based on grammatical gender.

twist.text: Finnish has no grammatical gender. Finnish speakers still hold gender stereotypes—just not about bridges.

climax.text: Countries with gendered languages show slightly wider gaps in gender roles, though causation is debated.

punchline.text: Grammar whispers biases we never chose.

quiz.question: Who demonstrated that grammatical gender affects object perception?

details.summary: Many languages assign gender to every noun — a bridge is feminine in German (die Brücke) and masculine in Spanish (el puente). Research shows this affects how speakers perceive objects: Germans describe bridges as elegant and slender while Spaniards describe them as strong and towering.
details.whyItMatters: Gendered grammar demonstrates that invisible linguistic structures shape thought in ways speakers are unaware of. It fuels debates about gender-neutral language reform.
takeaways: German feminine bridges are described as elegant; Spanish masculine bridges as strong
Gender-neutral language reforms face resistance in gendered-grammar languages
Swedish successfully introduced a gender-neutral pronoun (hen) in 2015

faq.question: Does grammatical gender affect how people think?
faq.answer: Yes. Lera Boroditsky and colleagues asked German and Spanish speakers to describe objects with opposite grammatical genders. Germans described a key (masculine in German) as hard, heavy, and useful; Spaniards described a key (feminine in Spanish) as golden, intricate, and lovely.

faq.question: Can gender-neutral language reform work?
faq.answer: Sweden's introduction of 'hen' (gender-neutral pronoun) in 2015 has been largely successful — it is now widely used and accepted. German's gender-neutral experiments (Gendersternchen: Student*innen) remain controversial. Spanish's Latinx faces resistance from native speakers.
